title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: what a Buddhist means by the breath
hook: the second visit: a Buddhist hall where the only instruction is to know you're breathing
carry: breathe the way you're already breathing
tomorrow: guided visits: what the Sufis mean by remembrance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first visit: a Sikh kitchen, and seva with no bill. Today the week's strand name, what a Buddhist means by the breath, becomes the visit.

A Buddhist meditation hall: a wooden floor, cushions in rows, a bell, a small statue of the Buddha at the front. You expect instructions. Relax your shoulders. Breathe in for four, hold for four. Picture a light. The teacher says none of that. She says: sit. Breathe the way you're already breathing. And know it. That's all? That's all. And people have spent their whole lives inside that one instruction. Today, the breath as the Buddhists who kept it for twenty-five centuries mean it.
screen: `A HALL, A BELL, CUSHIONS.` → `NO COUNTING, NO PICTURE.` → `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: The teaching comes from a discourse Buddhists call the Anapanasati Sutta, mindfulness of breathing, in the middle-length collection of the Buddha's talks. It opens almost like stage directions. A monk goes to the forest, or the root of a tree, or an empty hut. He sits with legs crossed and back straight, and sets mindfulness in front of him. Mindful, he breathes in. Mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in a long breath, he knows: I breathe in long. Breathing in a short breath, he knows: I breathe in short. That's the first surprise: nothing is being fixed. The long breath isn't better than the short one. The practice is knowing, not steering. The second surprise is how far it goes. The sutta lays out sixteen steps, from the length of the breath, through the whole body calming, then feelings, then the mind itself, to watching everything change and letting go. The Buddha says, in that text, that this one practice, developed, brings the four foundations of mindfulness to completion. The whole path, folded inside one breath. And why the breath? Because it's always here, and it never stays. Each breath is gone as it arrives. Buddhists call that anicca, impermanence, and the breath teaches it every four seconds without saying a word. The Buddhist door made the breath its second word, on day two. A guest just hears it their way: not a technique for power, but a place to know what's happening, right now.
screen: `MINDFUL, HE BREATHES IN.` · `KNOWING, NOT STEERING.` · `SIXTEEN STEPS, ONE BREATH.` · `EACH BREATH GONE AS IT ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit, back straight, the way the text describes, and don't change the breath: when it comes in long, know it's long; when it comes in short, know it's short. When your mind wanders off, and it will, notice that too, and come back to the next breath. No counting, no picture, no goal: just a guest sitting quietly in someone else's hall.
Anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing in and out. Not controlling it; knowing it, and watching it change.
Your line: breathe the way you're already breathing. See you at the third house tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 324 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT THE SUFIS MEAN BY REMEMBRANCE.`

howItsDone: Many Buddhists, in Theravada, Zen and Tibetan communities alike, practice mindfulness of breathing, sitting quietly and knowing each breath as it comes and goes, often in a hall with a bell to begin and end.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: ana and apana, the breath in and out, + sati, mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: breath meditation is a relaxation trick.
what it means: for Buddhists, knowing each breath as it is, a doorway to body, feeling, mind and impermanence.
what a scholar hears: the sutta's own verbs are assasati and passasati, breathing in and out, and the old Pali commentaries disagree on which of the two is the in-breath.
guess: knowing each breath as it comes, without steering it
slow, counted breathing to calm the body down
holding the breath to build up inner power

notes: The sutta's breathing lines are paraphrased close to the text, not quoted (Rhys Davids's wording for DN 22 was not verified word for word). A Buddhist reviewer should also see this day.
Trapdoor claim: the Visuddhimagga and the Vinaya commentary disagree on whether ana is the in-breath or the out-breath; please confirm.

Audit (second sample): the trapdoor said the commentaries disagree on which of 'ana and apana' is in and which is out. The disagreement the Visuddhimagga reports (VIII, on assāsa/passāsa: the Vinaya commentary takes assāsa as the out-breath, the Sutta commentary as the in-breath) is about the sutta's words assāsa and passāsa, so the floor now names those. Also fixed a tense slip in the teach ('was' to 'is').
'Twenty-five centuries' is the conventional rounding for the Buddha's dates (5th century BCE, dates debated).
